articles.title: Reeleito, Lula diz que venceu 'intromissão' de big techs e que vai mudar jeito de governar | G1
articles.standfirst: Petista afirmou que, no novo mandato, vai melhorar a comunicação digital e ampliar a participação popular. Também declarou que vai atuar em conjunto com o Congresso, apesar da forte oposição.
articles.summary: Petista afirmou que, no novo mandato, vai melhorar a comunicação digital e ampliar a participação popular. Também declarou que vai atuar em conjunto com o Congresso, apesar da forte oposição.
articles.body:
Reeleito presidente da República, após virada histórica, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) afirmou no seu primeiro discurso que ele e sua coligação tiveram de vencer o que chamou de "intromissão" externa de plataformas.

O presidente disse que, no novo mandato, vai mudar a forma de governar, com melhoria na comunicação digital e a ampliação da participação popular nas ações governamentais.

Na avenida Paulista, em novo discurso, a uma multidão que o aguardava, agradeceu a Deus e dedicou a virada aos jovens, às mulheres e aos trabalhadores (veja abaixo) .

Às vésperas de completar 81 anos, o que ocorrerá na próxima terça-feira (27), o petista se tornou, ao derrotar Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ), o primeiro presidente da história do Brasil a ser eleito quatro vezes pelo voto popular .

A confirmação da vitória de Lula foi feita pelo sistema do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), às 21h08 , quando 97% das urnas já tinham sido apuradas. Àquela altura, Lula tinha 51,74% e Flávio tinha 48,26% . Com a totalização das urnas às 23h30, Lula ficou com 51,79% e Flávio, 48,21%.

"Essa eleição foi uma eleição que a gente teve que vencer a intromissão, vinda de fora para dentro, através de plataformas digitais, que nós vamos ter que regulá-las. Não é possível que a gente não tenha consciência que o crime do mundo digital tenha que ser tratado igual ao crime da vida real", afirmou Lula.

Lula também disse que o resultado da eleição foi uma "derrota para o negacionismo e para a mentira". E fez críticas a Flávio Bolsonaro.

"Nunca pensei em me deparar com um representante genuíno do 'milicianismo' neste país. Nunca imaginei que uma pessoa pudesse mentir tanto, com tanta desfaçatez, como se não tivesse, dentro dele, uma célula de humanismo, parece tudo falso", afirmou.

O petista também disse que pretende desenvolver uma inteligência artificial brasileira. E agradeceu a integrantes da campanha, como o deputado André Janones ( Rede -MG), que coordenou o canal de WhatsApp "Exército do Lula", com mais de 10 milhões de inscritos, na campanha eleitoral.

"E quero dizer que uma coisa eu aprendi. Eu não vou falar aqui para vocês, mas essa eleição me ensinou muitas lições. Eu posso garantir para vocês que nós vamos mudar o jeito de governar esse país. Quero dizer para vocês que nós vamos fazer o povo participar mais das nossas decisões, a comunicação digital vai ganhar um espaço muito grande no meu governo", declarou.

Lula também falou sobre a oposição que deve enfrentar no Congresso Nacional, que será composto em grande parte por políticos que apoiaram Flávio Bolsonaro na eleição presidencial.

O petista minimizou o cenário de adversidade e disse que não escolheu o Congresso eleito. O presidente afirmou que governará em conjunto com os parlamentares.

"Se depender de mim, esse país só tem que ser civilizado, esse país tem uma Constituição. Ninguém é obrigado a gostar do presidente eleito, mas ele foi eleito para governar para todos e ele foi eleito para governar com base no respeito à Constituição", afirmou Lula.

"Na relação com o Congresso... Porque já tem gente falando que o Lula vai ter muita dificuldade para governar, porque o Congresso está muito conservador... Eu não escolhi o Congresso, foi o povo que escolheu e é com ele que eu vou votar, vou trabalhar e vou aprovar as coisas", afirmou.

Ele também disse que o quarto mandato será o melhor de todos que já teve.

'Corinthians parece o Bolsonaro, só perde'

Corinthiano, o presidente disse que conversará com todos os setores da sociedade, como empresários e cientistas, e até com o Corinthians. Nesse momento, ele aproveitou para alfinetar o adversário na eleição presidencial.

"Eu tenho dois meses pela frente, para discutir o governo, vou me reunir com empresários, educadores, cientistas, mulheres, o Corinthians também... O Corinthians perdeu outra, está parecendo o Bolsonaro, só perde", brincou Lula.

O petista fez uma referência à derrota do time paulistano no Campeonato Brasileiro neste sábado (24), quando o Corinthians foi derrotado por 3 a 2 pelo Vasco da Gama (RJ).

Lula deixou o hotel em direção à avenida Paulista, em São Paulo (SP), onde uma multidão o aguardava e comemorava a vitória do petista nas urnas por volta das 23h30. Pelo teto solar do carro que o transportava, falou aos apoiadores com um megafone.

Perto da meia-noite, Lula subiu em um trio elétrico e discursou em frente ao Museu de Arte de São Paulo (Masp). Ao lado do vice-presidente reeleito Geraldo Alckmin, prometeu a universalização do programa Pé-de-Meia no ensino médio, a criação do Pé-de-Meia Universitário e a ampliação do ensino integral.

Lula na avenida Paulista após reeleição. — Foto: Amanda Perobelli/Reuters

O petista voltou a exaltar a participação na campanha do deputado federal reeleito André Janones (Rede-MG), que esteve à frente da mobilização pela reeleição do presidente na internet. E agradeceu a atuação no segundo turno do senador e coordenador de campanha Camilo Santana e do governador reeleito do Piauí Rafael Fonteles.

Lula pediu que o "Hino da Independência" fosse tocado. "Quero pedir outra vez para tocar o 'Hino da Independência', para eles saberem que nós não cabemos no quintal de ninguém."

"Eu tenho dentro de mim um sentimento de gratidão. Eu posso dizer para vocês, acredito muito em Deus e acho que no dia que o povo brasileiro acordou e resolveu eleger metalúrgico sem diploma universitário presidente da República, foi o dedo de Deus que fez vocês confiarem que um operário poderia fazer mais que a elite brasileira tinha feito em 500 anos nesse país", afirmou o petista.

O presidente dedicou a virada nas urnas à "juventude rebelde que se levantou pela democracia", às mulheres e aos trabalhadores.

"Eu quero agradecer a cada homem, a cada mulher. Hoje, eu vi na televisão o gesto de muitos netos levando o avô e avó para votar em cadeira de roda. Eu devo essa vitória a juventude rebelde que se levantou em defesa da democracia. Eu devo essa vitória às mulheres que se rebelaram contra o feminicídio. Eu devo às pessoas que acreditam que o fim da escala 6 por 1 é um benefício pra sociedade brasileira. Eu devo essa vitória aos educadores que acreditam que a educação é a melhor solução para fazer o país falta de qualidade. Eu devo essa vitória a cada um e a cada uma de vocês", disse Lula.

articles.title: Lula tem 64 milhões de votos: compare com 2022 e Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Petista obteve 3.822.779 votos a mais do que recebeu em 2022 e obteve maioria no Norte e no Nordeste; candidato tornou-se o mais votado desde a redemocratização.
articles.summary: Lula alcançou votação recorde de 64 milhões de votos, superando Flávio Bolsonaro e seu desempenho de 2022 com vitórias decisivas no Norte e Nordeste.
articles.body:
Lula e Jair Bolsonaro. — Foto: Ton Molina/FotoArena/Estadão Conteúdo; Reuters/Adriano Machado

Com 64 milhões de votos, o presidente Lula (PT) foi reeleito na noite deste domingo (25) na disputa de segundo turno contra Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que obteve 59 milhões. O resultado foi declarado às 21h08 pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Com 100% das urnas apuradas, os números foram:

Lula - 64.256.232 votos (51,79% dos válidos)

Flávio Bolsonaro - 59.826.041 votos (48,21% dos válidos)

No segundo turno de 2022, os resultados foram:

Lula (PT) - 60.345.999 votos (50,90% dos válidos)

Jair Bolsonaro (PL) - 58.206.354 votos (49,10% dos válidos)

O primeiro turno de 2026 foi o mais apertado desde a redemocratização, com diferença de cerca de 2,1 milhões de votos em favor de Flávio Bolsonaro. Uma distância similar, mas ainda assim inferior, aos 2,2 milhões de votos a mais conquistados por Lula frente a Jair Bolsonaro no segundo turno de 2022.

Já no segundo turno deste ano, a vantagem de Lula passou para 4,4 milhões na disputa com Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). O petista obteve 3.822.779 votos a mais que em 2022.

Neste ano, Lula também superou o recorde havia estabelecido em 2022, quando obteve a maior votação desde a redemocratização.

Votos de Lula no 2º turno de 2022 - 60 milhões

Votos de Lula no 2º turno de 2026 - 64 milhões

A única região do país em que Lula venceu em 2022 foi o Nordeste, onde obteve 69,34% dos votos. Já a região Sul teve a maior vantagem de Jair Bolsonaro, que conquistou 61,84% dos votos válidos, ante 38,16% do aversário. Naquela disputa, Bolsonaro também venceu com folga no Centro-Oeste.

Em 2026, Lula manteve a liderança no Nordeste, com 69,37% dos votos. Também conquistou maioria no Norte, com 50% dos votos e diferença de cerca de mil votos. A região Sul permaneceu um reduto bolsonarista: Flávio chegou a 62,58% dos votos, ante 37,42% de Lula.

O candidato do PL também venceu no Sudeste, com 52,76% dos votos, e no Centro-Oeste, com 60,01%.

articles.title: Minas Gerais é o único estado onde a liderança na disputa presidencial mudou entre o 1º e o 2º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Flávio Bolsonaro foi o mais votado no estado no primeiro turno, mas Lula passou à frente no segundo. Nos outros 25 estados e no Distrito Federal, os candidatos mantiveram a liderança.
articles.summary: Flávio Bolsonaro foi o mais votado no estado no primeiro turno, mas Lula passou à frente no segundo. Nos outros 25 estados e no Distrito Federal, os candidatos mantiveram a liderança.
articles.body:
Minas Gerais foi o único estado brasileiro onde a liderança na disputa presidencial mudou entre o primeiro e o segundo turno das eleições de 2026 , realizado neste domingo (25). Segundo dados parciais do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), Lula (PT) ultrapassou Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que havia sido o candidato mais votado no estado no primeiro turno.

Na votação de 4 de outubro , Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 48,24% dos votos válidos em Minas Gerais, enquanto Lula ficou com 43,33%.

Apoiadores de Lula comemoram reeleição em Belo Horizonte — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Neste domingo, o cenário se inverteu. Com 99,76% das seções totalizadas, Lula registrava 50,40% dos votos válidos, contra 49,60% de Flávio Bolsonaro . Os números foram atualizados às 21h52.

A diferença entre os dois candidatos no estado era de 0,80 ponto percentual no segundo turno.

Nos outros 25 estados e no Distrito Federal, não houve mudança de liderança . O candidato que terminou o primeiro turno à frente também recebeu a maior parcela dos votos válidos no segundo.

A mudança ocorreu justamente em um estado que mantém uma tradição nas eleições presidenciais brasileiras : desde 1989, todos os candidatos eleitos para a Presidência da República também foram os mais votados em Minas Gerais.

Em 2022, o petista já havia vencido no estado, com 50,20% dos votos válidos, contra 49,80% de Jair Bolsonaro (PL). Naquele ano, também conquistou a Presidência, com 50,90% dos votos válidos em todo o país.

Como ficou a liderança nos demais estados

No segundo turno, Flávio Bolsonaro manteve a liderança em 14 unidades da federação: Acre, Distrito Federal, Espírito Santo, Goiás, Mato Grosso, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná, Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Sul, Rondônia, Roraima, Santa Catarina, São Paulo e Tocantins.

Lula, por sua vez, permaneceu à frente em 12 estados: Alagoas, Amapá, Amazonas, Bahia, Ceará, Maranhão, Pará, Paraíba, Pernambuco, Piauí, Rio Grande do Norte e Sergipe.

Com a mudança em Minas Gerais, Lula passou a liderar em 13 estados no segundo turno, enquanto Flávio Bolsonaro ficou à frente em 13 estados e no Distrito Federal.

Os dados consideram a apuração disponível até as 21h54 deste domingo e podem sofrer alterações até a conclusão da totalização.

articles.title: Lula iguala recorde histórico de Franklin Roosevelt, presidente dos EUA, ao chegar ao 4º mandato | G1
articles.standfirst: Petista foi eleito quatro vezes pelo voto popular, assim como o ex-presidente dos Estados Unidos, que governou o país entre 1933 e 1945. Professor de Ciência Política da FGV aponta que os dois se equiparam quando consideradas eleições democráticas.
articles.summary: Petista foi eleito quatro vezes pelo voto popular, assim como o ex-presidente dos Estados Unidos, que governou o país entre 1933 e 1945. Professor de Ciência Política da FGV aponta que os dois se equiparam quando consideradas eleições democráticas.
articles.body:
Lula vota em São Bernardo do Campo (SP) — Foto: NELSON ALMEIDA/AFP

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) se tornou o presidente com o maior número de mandatos conquistados pelo voto popular em democracias , ao lado do ex-presidente dos Estados Unidos Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Com a vitória nas eleições deste domingo (25), o petista chegou ao quarto mandato à frente do Palácio do Planalto, igualando o recorde do americano, que governou o país por 12 anos, entre 1933 e 1945.

Até então, Roosevelt era o único nome entre os eleitos quatro vezes em democracias. Lula foi eleito em 2002 e 2006, voltou à Presidência em 2022 e conquistou um novo mandato em 2026.

Segundo Eduardo José Grin, professor de Ciência Política da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), a vitória de Lula o coloca no mesmo patamar histórico de Roosevelt quando são considerados os regimes democráticos com eleições competitivas .

"Em eleições onde tem competição aberta, disputa, que garante a sociedade poder se manifestar sem restrição, o Lula agora se equipara ao Franklin Roosevelt, dos Estados Unidos, como presidente que se elege por um quarto mandato", afirmou o professor ao g1.

"Não estou falando, por exemplo, de sucessões consecutivas na Venezuela ou na Rússia, onde a gente poderia chamar isso, de acordo com a literatura, de autocracias eleitorais ou autocracias competitivas", completou Grin.

O caso norte-americano tem uma particularidade histórica: quando Roosevelt conquistou seu terceiro e quarto mandatos, não existia uma regra constitucional que limitasse a quantidade de vezes que uma pessoa poderia ser eleita presidente dos Estados Unidos.

A situação mudou posteriormente. Em 1947, foi aprovada uma emenda constitucional que estabeleceu o limite de dois mandatos presidenciais no país.

No Brasil, um presidente pode exercer dois mandatos consecutivos, mas não pode disputar imediatamente um terceiro mandato seguido. A legislação, porém, permite que um ex-presidente volte a concorrer depois de deixar o cargo por um período, como ocorreu com Lula, que retornou ao Planalto em 2023 após vencer o Jair Bolsonaro (PL) nas eleições de 2022.

A política na vida de Lula em São Bernardo do Campo

Lula nasceu em 27 de outubro de 1945, em Garanhuns, no interior de Pernambuco. É o sétimo dos oito filhos do casal de lavradores Aristides Inácio da Silva e Eurídice Ferreira de Mello, conhecida como dona Lindu.

Seu pai deixou Pernambuco quando Lula ainda era bebê e se mudou para o litoral paulista em busca de trabalho. Em dezembro de 1952, aos sete anos, Lula viajou com a mãe e os irmãos para São Paulo em um caminhão pau de arara.

A família se instalou inicialmente no Guarujá, onde reencontrou Aristides, que já havia formado outra família. Dona Lindu acabou se separando do marido. Em 1956, ela e os filhos se mudaram para a capital paulista, onde passaram a morar em um pequeno cômodo nos fundos de um bar.

Lula durante greve de metalúrgicos em São Bernardo — Foto: Divulgação

Durante a infância e a adolescência, Lula trabalhou como vendedor ambulante, engraxate e office boy, até conseguir emprego na Fábrica de Parafusos Marte.

Aos 14 anos, ingressou na indústria. Aos 18, concluiu o curso de torneiro mecânico pelo Serviço Nacional de Aprendizagem Industrial (Senai). Antes disso, aos 17 anos, perdeu o dedo mínimo da mão esquerda em um acidente de trabalho.

Em 1969, casou-se com a operária Maria de Lourdes da Silva, que morreu grávida em 1971. Em 1974, casou-se com Marisa Letícia, com quem viveu por mais de quatro décadas.

Lula trabalhou na Indústria Villares, metalúrgica em São Bernardo do Campo, na região do ABC paulista. Sua entrada no movimento sindical ocorreu por influência do irmão José, conhecido como Frei Chico.

Ele ocupou diferentes funções no Sindicato dos Metalúrgicos de São Bernardo do Campo e Diadema, onde foi suplente, primeiro-secretário e presidente.

A atuação sindical ganhou projeção nacional durante as greves de metalúrgicos que paralisaram o ABC paulista no fim da década de 1970 e no início da década de 1980, durante a ditadura militar (1964-1985).

Em 1980, Lula foi preso por 31 dias com base na antiga Lei de Segurança Nacional, em uma reação do governo militar às mobilizações sindicais.

Naquele mesmo ano, foi um dos fundadores do Partido dos Trabalhadores, criado com a participação de políticos, sindicalistas, intelectuais, lideranças rurais e religiosas . Marisa Letícia, sua esposa na época, costurou a primeira bandeira do partido.

Lula também teve participação importante na criação da Central Única dos Trabalhadores (CUT), em 1983. No ano seguinte, participou da campanha das Diretas Já, movimento que levou multidões às ruas para exigir a retomada das eleições diretas para presidente da República.

A passagem do sindicalismo para a política eleitoral havia começado em 1982, quando Lula disputou o governo de São Paulo, sem sucesso, e terminou em quarto lugar.

Em 1986, foi eleito deputado federal por São Paulo e participou da Assembleia Nacional Constituinte, responsável pela elaboração da Constituição de 1988.

A trajetória eleitoral de Lula teve derrotas antes da primeira vitória presidencial. Depois de disputar eleições presidenciais sem sucesso, o petista chegou ao Palácio do Planalto em 2003, após vencer a eleição de 2002.

Ele foi reeleito em 2006 e permaneceu na Presidência até 2010. Depois de 12 anos fora do cargo, voltou a disputar a eleição presidencial e venceu Jair Bolsonaro em 2022, reassumindo o governo em janeiro de 2023.

A trajetória também foi marcada por condenações posteriormente anuladas pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e pelos 580 dias em que ficou preso. Após recuperar seus direitos políticos, Lula voltou à disputa eleitoral e conquistou o terceiro mandato presidencial em 2022.

articles.title: Veja as 10 cidades com menor abstenção no 2º turno e o que mudou em relação ao 1º turno e 2022 | G1
articles.standfirst: Bela Vista do Piauí registrou a menor taxa do país, com apenas 6,88% de eleitores ausentes. Nas dez cidades do ranking, a abstenção caiu em relação ao primeiro turno de 2026.
articles.summary: Bela Vista do Piauí registrou a menor taxa do país, com apenas 6,88% de eleitores ausentes. Nas dez cidades do ranking, a abstenção caiu em relação ao primeiro turno de 2026.
articles.body:
Prefeitura Municipal de Bela Vista do Piauí — Foto: Divulgação/Prefeitura de Bela Vista

Bela Vista do Piauí (PI), Rio Fortuna (SC) e São Jorge (RS) registraram as menores taxas de abstenção no segundo turno das eleições de 2026 , realizado neste domingo (25), segundo dados da Justiça Eleitoral.

Em Bela Vista do Piauí, apenas 6,88% dos eleitores deixaram de comparecer às urnas , o equivalente a 238 pessoas. O município também havia registrado a menor abstenção do país no primeiro turno, quando 7,31% dos eleitores não votaram, um total de 253 pessoas.

Na segunda posição aparece Rio Fortuna, em Santa Catarina, com 7,91% de abstenção (346 eleitores), seguida por São Jorge, no Rio Grande do Sul, com 8,90% (217 eleitores).

Todas as dez cidades com menor abstenção neste domingo tiveram redução na proporção de eleitores ausentes em relação ao primeiro turno de 2026.

A maior queda ocorreu em Riacho das Almas (PE), onde o percentual passou de 13,03% para 9,79%, uma redução de 3,24 pontos percentuais. Em São Jorge (RS), a abstenção caiu de 11,98% para 8,90%, diferença de 3,08 pontos percentuais.

Já na comparação com o segundo turno de 2022, sete das dez cidades registraram queda na abstenção. As exceções foram Nova Candelária, Santa Maria do Herval e Cândido Godói, todas no Rio Grande do Sul.

10 cidades com menor abstenção e a comparação com eleições anteriores

Bela Vista do Piauí também apresentou redução da abstenção na comparação com a última eleição presidencial . Em 2022, 9,02% dos eleitores do município não compareceram às urnas no segundo turno. Neste domingo, foram 6,88%, uma diferença de 2,14 pontos percentuais.

Entre as dez cidades analisadas, a maior redução em relação a 2022 ocorreu em Cunhataí (SC) , onde a taxa caiu de 12,09% para 9,63%, uma diferença de 2,46 pontos percentuais.

Por outro lado, três municípios gaúchos registraram aumento da abstenção na comparação com quatro anos atrás.

Em Cândido Godói, o percentual passou de 9,07% para 9,81%. Em Nova Candelária, subiu de 8,44% para 9,12%. Já em Santa Maria do Herval, a taxa passou de 8,93% para 9,54%.

Apesar dos aumentos em relação a 2022, os três municípios apresentaram queda na abstenção entre o primeiro e o segundo turno de 2026.

Sul concentra oito das dez cidades com menor abstenção

O ranking deste domingo também mostra uma concentração de municípios da Região Sul entre aqueles com as menores taxas de abstenção do país.

Das dez cidades, oito ficam no Sul : quatro em Santa Catarina e quatro no Rio Grande do Sul. As outras duas são Bela Vista do Piauí (PI), no Nordeste, e Riacho das Almas (PE), também no Nordeste.

articles.summary: Consulte a votação de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro nos municípios. Petista foi reeleito; resultados locais serão atualizados conforme a conclusão da apuração.
articles.body:
Lula (PT) foi reeleito presidente neste domingo (25) na disputa contra Flávio Bolsonaro (PL). O mapa abaixo mostra o candidato mais votado e seu percentual de votos válidos nas cidades brasileiras com apuração concluída.

No resultado nacional do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), concluído às 23h26 de domingo, Lula recebeu 64.256.232 votos, ou 51,79% dos válidos. Flávio Bolsonaro somou 59.826.041 votos, equivalentes a 48,21%.

🔎 A Presidência é definida pela soma dos votos válidos no Brasil e no exterior. Votos brancos e nulos não entram no cálculo dos percentuais dos candidatos.

MAPA - Como cada cidade votou para presidente no segundo turno de 2026 — Foto: Arte/g1

Lula foi o mais votado em 2.874 municípios, e Flávio, em 2.694. Em Marquinho, no Paraná, houve empate: cada candidato recebeu 1.530 votos, ou 50% dos válidos.

A contagem considera os 5.569 municípios, todos com apuração concluída. Brasília, Fernando de Noronha e as localidades de votação no exterior não entram nesse total.

O número de municípios vencidos não determina o resultado da eleição: cada cidade tem uma quantidade diferente de eleitores, e todos os votos válidos são somados para definir o vencedor nacional.

Nas capitais, Lula foi o mais votado em São Paulo (55,50%), Rio de Janeiro (51,54%) e Porto Alegre (55,84%), todas com apuração concluída. Flávio Bolsonaro venceu em Belo Horizonte (50,80%), Curitiba (62,29%) e Florianópolis (51,66%).

No Nordeste, Lula venceu em oito das nove capitais. A exceção foi Maceió, onde Flávio Bolsonaro recebeu 52,01% dos votos válidos.

No Norte, Lula venceu em Belém e Macapá, enquanto Flávio foi o mais votado em Manaus, Boa Vista, Porto Velho, Rio Branco e Palmas. O candidato do PL também venceu nas três capitais estaduais do Centro-Oeste, Goiânia, Cuiabá e Campo Grande, e em Brasília.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race becomes a test of Trump’s turnout machine
articles.summary: President Trump’s campaign stop in Mississippi on Monday is putting the ruby-red state in the spotlight as Democrats grow optimistic about their chances in the state’s Senate race. The Republican National Committee said Wednesday that Trump will headline a rally in the city of Corinth in northeastern Mississippi. Meanwhile, the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC announced…
articles.body:
President Trump’s campaign stop in Mississippi on Monday is putting the ruby-red state in the spotlight as Democrats grow optimistic about their chances in the state’s Senate race.

The Republican National Committee said Wednesday that Trump will headline a rally in the city of Corinth in northeastern Mississippi. Meanwhile, the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC announced it will spend $1.2 million in a television ad touting Democrat Scott Colom, who is challenging incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.). The Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund is spending more than $1 million in an effort to defend Hyde-Smith’s seat.

Colom, for his part, has taken advantage of the upcoming presidential campaign stop, challenging Trump to a debate.

The race is still an uphill climb for Mississippi Democrats, with the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rating the race as “likely Republican” after the election handicapper notably moved the race from “solid Republican” toward Democrats.

Democrats say they see some cause for hope in the state amid Trump’s poor approval ratings, while Republicans look to replicate their national turnout strategy in the deep-red state.

“I don’t think Republican voters are going to go vote for Scott Colom in any big number,” said Austin Barbour, a Mississippi-based Republican strategist.

“What they could do is they could say, ‘Hey, I’m not showing up that day,’” Barbour added.

The move to deploy Trump to northeastern Mississippi is notable, given the region is highly saturated with the president’s supporters. Corinth is located in the state’s 1st Congressional District, which the president carried with 68 percent of the vote in 2024.

Trump’s Mississippi visit follows a number of trips from high-profile Democrats meant to galvanize the party’s base.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris and Sens. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) and Cory Booker (D-N.J.) have all made stops in Mississippi this month.

Former President Obama, arguably the Democratic Party’s strongest turnout asset, separately cut a 30-second ad for Colom.

The visits from Obama, Harris, Warnock and Booker are seen as part of a strategy to galvanize Mississippi’s Black voters, who make up 36 percent of the state’s population. That’s the largest of any state.

“African American voters tend to vote 90-plus percent for Democratic candidates,” Barbour said. “If you’re down voting in Mississippi, you start out with a significant voting bloc, so it’s a turnout game as every election is.”

Barbour argued that the national attention from Democrats, along with Trump’s visit, is enough to wake up the state’s Republican base, including low-propensity voters.

“They also are starting to realize just because we’re pissed off, that doesn’t mean we can just stay home, or skip this race and allow a guy who admittedly says he’s a far-left candidate, represent Mississippi in the United States Senate,” he said.

Mississippi-based Republican strategist Hayes Dent noted the presence of the national Democrats could backfire.

“If Scott had really wanted to win the race, and if the Democrats had really thought that this race was competitive, you wouldn’t have seen those folks campaigning in Mississippi,” Dent said.

However, Dent acknowledged there was still a high level of frustration among Republicans over Trump’s economic policies and the Iran war.

“When you go and tell everybody you’re going to get us out of wars, you’re going to drain the swamp, you’re going to cut gas prices, you’re going to do all of this, and none of that is occurring, people get frustrated,” Dent said.

Like other states, Mississippi’s agriculture sector has also been hit hard by high fuel prices.

Average diesel prices in Mississippi reached a record high of $6.06 per gallon last month, and today they sit at $5.86, according to AAA .

Earlier this week, the state’s agriculture commissioner called on Mississippi leaders to suspend the state’s fuel tax to bring relief.

“When you layer tariffs and then put what might be a current cherry on top by saying you’re trying to harvest your crop by paying $6 a gallon for diesel fuel, your politics sort of go out the window for maybe one of the truest phrases ever, which is ‘it’s the economy, stupid,'” Dent said.

According to a Civiqs tracking poll, Trump’s approval rating in the state sits at 41 percent while his disapproval rating is at 52 percent.

Public polling in the race has been scarce, but polling commissioned by Democrats paints a rosy picture.

An internal poll released from the left-leaning Change Research showed Hyde-Smith leading Colom with 43 percent support to his 40 percent, with a 3.5 point margin of error. A poll from the progressive Data for Progress released in August showed Hyde-Smith leading Colom with 44 percent support to his 38 percent, with a 3-point margin of error.

The state also recently saw a highly competitive statewide race in 2023, where Gov. Tate Reeves (R) defeated Democrat Brandon Presley by just more than 3 points.

Democrats are also pointing to other traditionally red states in the South that have shown movement toward Democrats including Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina.

However, unlike those states, Democrats note Mississippi would prove much harder to flip.

“I think it’s going to be closer than normal,” said one Democratic strategist. “But still a hard piece of candy to eat.”

The Republican Senate campaign arm called Colom “out of touch” for campaigning with Harris in the state.

“Scott Colom is a Chuck Schumer-backed, George Soros-funded, Transgender Defender so out of touch with Mississippi that he is campaigning with Kamala Harris, who lost the state by 22 points,” said Samantha Cantrell, regional press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

A GOP official brushed off the notion there was any concern about Mississippi, calling Democratic spending in the state “a pipe dream.”

“The easiest way to extinguish any doubt is to hold a rally and energize Republican voters,” the GOP official said.

“We’re confident Mississippi will stay red and any Democrats or anonymous Republican operatives who tell you otherwise are high on their own supply,” the official added.

articles.title: Planting false information in the news? It’s much easier than you think.
articles.summary: Faulty midterm polling is bad enough, but it actually gets much worse.
articles.body:
It shouldn’t be this easy for false information to worm its way into mainstream news reporting. But it is.

Several news outlets and polling aggregators were embarrassed last week after a new polling firm, Wedgewood Polling, was revealed to be a hoax operation. The firm had produced dozens of fabricated voter surveys, many of which favored Democratic candidates.

Wedgewood now claims it was merely conducting a social experiment, to show how easily phony data can enter into election coverage. The victims of the Wedgewood hoax are many, including Nate Silver’s Silver Bulletin, USA Today, Newsweek, and the New York Times, which removed 15 of the organization’s baloney polls from its tracking page and issued an editor’s note.

The Wedgewood incident is, unfortunately, not unique. It is representative of a much deeper, more serious problem in media. Bad information, whether deliberate or accidental, routinely slips into mainstream reporting, touching subjects well beyond midterm elections, and often shaping political beliefs, health decisions, and even legislation.

Consider the much-publicized claim that the right is responsible for most of the political violence in the U.S. Back when this claim first reared its head, it got plenty of play in the press. The problem is that the underlying study is nonsense. The “right” is responsible for the lion’s share of all U.S. political violence – so long as we count prison fights as “political violence” and we classify inmates as “right-wing .” Note that no other group is held to this standard.

It is a joke of a study — did anyone even read it? But it has had no trouble drawing frequent and breathless coverage.

The episode recalls 2018, when major media uncritically promoted Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s DNA test as proof of her Native American ancestry . “A DNA analysis done on Sen. Elizabeth Warren provides strong evidence she has Native American heritage, a claim her critics have long mocked,” declared the Associated Press.

Some coverage even took a tone of smug righteousness aimed squarely at President Trump, who had mocked Warren’s claimed ancestry.

“The Trump [administration], for the second time in 12 hours: Don’t believe science,” wrote Aaron Blake, then Washington Post senior political reporter. But then readers did what the journalists and headline writers had apparently failed to do: They actually read the DNA report and found that Warren was six to ten generations removed from any Native American ancestry — at best between 1/64th and 1/1,024th Native American. Looks like someone didn’t read past the executive summary.

The DNA episode was itself reminiscent of an earlier incident from 2015, in which news outlets fell for a hoax study claiming people could lose weight simply by eating chocolate. That study was part of a broader experiment testing reporters’ ability to detect junk science. They failed, of course. The supposed findings appeared in news articles instantly without a trace of skepticism — in the Daily Mail, HuffPo, Modern Healthcare and others.

“Our point was not that journalists could be tricked by fakers, but rather that scientists themselves in this field and other fields are making the kinds of mistakes that we made on purpose,” the study’s author, a journalist whose real first name is John, told me at the time .

“This whole area of science has become kind of corrupted by really poor standards between scientists and journalists,” he added. “There are smart people out there who are getting fooled by this stuff because they think scientists know what they’re doing.”

But boy, some scientists clearly have no idea what they’re talking about or are just making stuff up — yet their predictions are regularly treated as authoritative. These claims, routinely elevated without question, are often the most dangerous.

Recall, for example, the quack Paul R. Ehrlich . He predicted in the mid-20th century that overpopulation would cause mass food shortages, depleted resources, riots, and global famine by the 1970s and 1980s. In 1970, he predicted that four billion people would die over the next 20 years from food and resource shortages.

Nothing he predicted happened — just the opposite. Ehrlich’s claims nevertheless enjoyed a certain level of legitimacy because they were covered as straight news. People believed him because the media propped him up. Some even choose not to have children precisely because they believed his predictions about overpopulation.

The media elevation of Ehrlich was not an isolated event. We have been fed a steady diet of such doomer kookery for decades, including headlines that read, “Earth is likely to cross a critical global warming threshold within the next decade unless drastic changes are made” (2023); “[M]ajor European cities will be sunk beneath rising seas as Britain is plunged into a ‘Siberian’ climate by 2020” (2004); “U.N. Predicts Disaster If Global Warming Not Checked” (1989); “U.S. scientist sees new ice age coming” (1971); “Expert says Arctic Ocean will soon be an open sea; catastrophic shifts in climate feared if change occurs; other specialists see no thinning of polar ice cap” (1969), and “Warming Arctic climate melting glaciers faster, raising ocean level, scientist says” (1947).

It shouldn’t be so easy for bogus, faulty, and flat-out incorrect information to make its way into the news flow. But this is the world we live in.

Sometimes, reporters are lazy or face deadline pressure. Sometimes they just don’t understand the material; they merely accept the toplines and trust the author as both honest and competent. Sometimes the journalist himself is dishonest.

The sources of bad information also vary. Sometimes the error is honest. Sometimes, a committed ideologue presents a sincerely held but flawed conclusion. Sometimes it’s the worst-case scenario: a bad faith actor feeding propaganda into the media megaphone.

Whether the fault lies with the journalist or the source, the result is the same: A falsehood gains legitimacy, latching onto the reputation of a credible news organization, and makes its way around the world a half-dozen times before anyone realizes anything is wrong.

Faulty midterm polling is one thing. Far more consequential is the ease with which fake facts and junk science on existential questions evade closer media scrutiny, slipping past the media gatekeepers and right into the ear of your congressman or president.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Trump takes blow in Brazil; faces new challenge in Venezuela
articles.summary: In today’s issue: President Trump‘s South America policy suffered setbacks on Sunday as a key ally took a stunning defeat in Brazil and Venezuela’s top opposition leader returned to her home country to challenge its Trump-backed leader. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a decisive comeback to win another term as president in its runoff after…
articles.body:
President Trump ‘s South America policy suffered setbacks on Sunday as a key ally took a stunning defeat in Brazil and Venezuela’s top opposition leader returned to her home country to challenge its Trump-backed leader.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off a decisive comeback to win another term as president in its runoff after having trailed in the first round of the election earlier this month. Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro , the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro , who is serving a prison sentence for his role in attempting to overturn the last election’s results.

Trump hadn’t directly weighed in on the race, but the younger Bolsonaro’s election would have elevated another Trump ally in South America, which has seen a rightward shift in its elections in recent years.

Right-wing leaders have won presidential elections in several neighboring South American countries in just the past year — José Antonio Kast in Chile, Keiko Fujimori in Peru and Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia. All of them have pushed for closer relations with the Trump administration.

But that trend was bucked in Brazil, where Lula has shown resistance to working with the administration on its priorities.

One of those key points of tension has been Lula’s refusal to join the U.S. operation to target drug cartels in Central and South America.

Lula warned in May after the U.S. designated Brazil’s two largest criminal factions as terrorist groups that this could become a pretext for U.S. intervention.

“We don’t accept being treated like children,” he said, maintaining that Brazilian forces would fight the groups themselves.

Tensions have also sparked over the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally whom Lula defeated for reelection in 2022. Just as Trump has refused to acknowledge his loss in the 2020 presidential election, the older Bolsonaro refused to accept his defeat.

Bolsonaro’s supporters stormed Brazil’s government buildings in the capital in an insurrection responding to Lula’s inauguration in January 2023, an incident that drew comparisons to the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot in the U.S. Bolsonaro was ultimately prosecuted over the coup plot and handed a 27-year prison sentence.

Trump has levied significant tariffs on Brazil to get the country to stand down in its prosecution of Bolsonaro, but these attempts have been unsuccessful.

The younger Bolsonaro is also refusing to concede his loss to Lula, calling for the results to be annulled. He’s pointing to a late court decision that ordered the polling times to be extended by two hours in response to issues with voter transport.

Trump hasn’t responded yet to the results of the election. At the same time, he’s now facing a more complex situation in Venezuela, where he has been working with a more friendly leader since U.S. forces deposed and captured former leader Nicolás Maduro in January.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to her home country Sunday after 10 months in exile.

This marks Machado’s first appearance in Venezuela since Maduro’s ouster. Maduro’s vice president Delcy Rodríguez has served as acting president since then, with America’s backing.

Rodríguez hasn’t changed many authoritarian policies of the Maduro regime internally, but she has made agreements giving the U.S. greater access to Venezuela’s vast array of oil reserves, a key priority for the Trump administration.

Trump has a complicated relationship with Machado. He has supported her movement to challenge Maduro in the past but has declined to back her to become Venezuela’s new leader, arguing she “doesn’t have the support” she needs within the country.

Machado has made strides to develop her relationship with Trump, presenting her Nobel Peace Prize medal to him in January, an award that he badly wants. But that hasn’t changed his posture in who should be leading Venezuela.

Her return to Venezuela will almost certainly up the pressure on Rodríguez to hold elections and put the Trump administration in a complicated spot between an ally and the current leader of the country, who has proven pliable to U.S. demands.

Machado has previously said she would run for president if elections are held in Venezuela before the end of the year. Rodríguez has not yet scheduled elections since taking over, even as her presidency was only supposed to be a short-term measure.

“Estoy aquí. Con ustedes,” Machado wrote in a post on the social platform X addressed to the Venezuelan people, which translates to “I am here. With you.”

CALL FOR NOMINATIONS : The Hill is currently collecting nominations for its annual Top Lobbyists list, made up of the most influential folks in Washington. Know a lobbyist who moved the needle this year? Nominate them for The Hill’s Top Lobbyists here by Nov. 6.

Trump confirmed he is considering moving the White House press briefing room from its longstanding location to somewhere else so he can use the spot for “badly needed space.” He previously denied a New York Times report that he spoke to aides about moving the room to bring back the indoor swimming pool that was covered decades ago to make space for the briefing room.

A federal appeals court appeared resistant to immediately agree to the Trump administration’s push to segregate 20,000 California ballots it says are likely noncitizen voters. The panel seemed skeptical that it needed to direct a trial judge to move quicker on the issue.

Serbia’s strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in parliamentary elections Sunday to a new political grouping called Student List-Students Win. “It is clear that we have lost these elections,” he said, in a surprisingly gracious statement after two years of battling student-led street protests .

SOUTHERN HOSPITALITY : The president’s midterm campaign tour will move down south today when he rallies with Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) in the historical Republican stronghold of Mississippi.

The rally was a late addition to Trump’s final blitz. Hyde-Smith is seeking to fend off a challenge from Democrat Scott Colom and is favored, but Democrats nationally see some chance of pulling off an upset.

The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC has announced it’s spending $1.2 million on a television ad for Colom. The GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund is meanwhile spending more than $1 million to defend the incumbent.

Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Julia Manchester about how the race is becoming a test of Trump’s turnout machine among Republican voters in a ruby red state.

Trump’s visit will come after a busy weekend, which he wrapped up in Michigan on Sunday with a rally for former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), who is running for Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed .

Former President Obama campaigned in Michigan and Ohio for slates of Democratic candidates on Saturday, ripping Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

▪ The Hill : Why a blue wave might miss Minnesota’s Senate race.

SHAKEN UP: Alaska Senate Democratic candidate Mary Peltola announced she would reschedule campaign events after she was in a car crash that resulted in minor injuries .

The campaign said the vehicle that she and her family were traveling in to a campaign stop was struck by another driver.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” wrote Cheryl Bruce , Peltola’s campaign manager.

“Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families,” he added.

She will begin campaigning again Tuesday with a stop in Homer, Alaska.

The Anchorage Police Department said, “The circumstances of the collision are under investigation.”

READY TO GO : The U.S. military has drafted plans to potentially strike Iran following the midterms, a source aware of the plans told The Hill’s Filip Timotija .

The source said U.S. Central Command (Centcom), which oversees U.S. forces in the Middle East, has plans ready to conduct follow-up strikes if it receives authorization from the White House. Centcom has multiple options for strikes in place, another source said.

Direct strikes against Iran have been on hiatus while the U.S. has focused on economic pressure to extract concessions from Tehran. Trump has personally warned the U.S. could attack again after the elections amid stalled diplomatic negotiations.

Iran’s economy is in tatters amid economic sanctions and U.S. naval blockade. However, Tehran has shown no signs of caving to U.S. demands. And Americans are feeling the pain too, with soaring oil and gas prices driving broader inflation.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump’s farm lifeline won’t fully solve farmers’ diesel problem.

▪ Reuters : Iran has ramped up efforts to target U.S. personnel.

The president will meet with U.S. Ambassador to France and Monaco Charles Kushner at 1:30 p.m. He will travel to Corinth, Miss., to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. EDT and then return to the White House.

The House will convene at 12:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 5:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

WHY WAIT : Early voting is surging in several key battleground states as Democrats hope to build a firewall ahead of Election Day that will advantage them in the midterms.

Morning Report co-writer Sarah Fortinsky reports that more than 23 million ballots have been cast nationwide , as of this weekend, compared with more than 15 million at a similar point in the 2022 midterm cycle.

The increase, which includes both in-person and mail-in ballots, has been driven by a 47 percent jump among registered Democrats and a 60 percent jump among unaffiliated voters. Early voting among Republicans is up 2.6 percent.

A New York Times analysis of state election records and voter data through Thursday showed early voting was up 69 percent in Kansas, 41 percent in Maine and 24 percent in Iowa — crucial states in the battle for Senate control.

“It’s the same pattern. Democrats and unaffiliateds are engaged. Republicans are not as engaged,” Michael McDonald , a political science professor at the University of Florida who tracks early voting, told Sarah. “And it explains why you might be seeing this shift of the battleground into these red states. Overall, there’s just more engagement among Democrats.”

Still, there are limitations to how much can be extrapolated from the data. McDonald noted that various factors can affect states’ early voting numbers, including changing timelines for when mail-in ballots are sent out.

Not all states record party registration, and a voter’s registration doesn’t guarantee which candidate they will support.

articles.title: The House is sitting on the evidence about pulsed microwave attacks
articles.summary: Two years ago, I implored Congress and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence specifically to allow me to brief them on evidence the U.S. government possesses of pulsed microwave attacks allegedly perpetrated by Russia, causing so-called Havana Syndrome. These attacks have injured hundreds of U.S. government personnel, including myself, my wife and my two…
articles.body:
Two years ago, I implored Congress and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence specifically to allow me to brief them on evidence the U.S. government possesses of pulsed microwave attacks allegedly perpetrated by Russia, causing so-called Havana Syndrome . These attacks have injured hundreds of U.S. government personnel, including myself, my wife and my two children.

Just weeks after I wrote that oped, the State Department retaliated against me . The retaliation became more intense after I praised House Intel Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) for allowing me the opportunity to testify about the Havana Syndrome coverup by the State Department and Intelligence Community.

I testified with the expectation that the committee would do as it had promised — hold officials accountable for, among other things, willful negligence and denied medical care that led to many of our traumatic brain injuries (especially those of my two children) being much worse than they should have been.

After the testimony of dozens of injured and non-injured officials with knowledge of the U.S. Intelligence Community and State Department coverup of these pulsed microwave attacks, the committee has produced a bombshell report . In any previous Congress, this report would have been released months ago and resulted in some real accountability.

But in a betrayal of all those injured — and especially of those who testified and faced illegal retaliation for doing so — Crawford inexplicably refuses to release his committee’s report . Why would House Intelligence do this after committing so much time and colossal congressional effort , promising accountability to the victims of these pulsed microwave attacks?

The committee leadership claims that the CIA is slow-rolling the declassification process of the congressional report. Of course they are — the report is surely damning to many of CIA’s senior leadership . What is deplorable is that Congress would let the agency get away with such dilatory tactics, deferring to the same people behind the wrongdoing and retaliation it is investigating.

This absurd situation is made even worse because the committee, like all committees in this Congress, is seemingly taking direction from the White House. The administration may not want this report released because it likely ties Russia to these attacks against U.S. personnel. I am far from being alone in believing the State Department and U.S. intelligence community possess evidence of Russian involvement but are avoiding releasing it. As someone personally affected by this, I want the truth to be revealed.

This would certainly not be the first betrayal in history by a politician, but all the committee has to do is release its own report. Instead of treating Russian President Vladimir Putin with the deference that the executive branch seems to want, the committee should exercise a modicum of independence and conduct some real oversight for a change. The fact that members would sit on this information sets a troubling precedent that should concern every U.S. citizen.

Until he is publicly held accountably by Congress, Putin will continue to be treated like a friend of this White House and receive invites to visit the U.S. Each time that happens, take a moment to consider the role Russia played in inflicting horrific brain injuries on U.S. government personnel using directed energy attacks.

Mark Lenzi is former spokesman for the New Hampshire Republican Party and a former country director for the International Republican Institute. He works for the U.S. State Department’s Diplomatic Security Service. He is currently receiving traumatic brain injury treatment at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center for injuries received while serving abroad. His views do not necessarily reflect those of the U.S. government.

articles.title: Corporations enabling Trump’s corruption deserve ‘pocketbook justice’
articles.summary: Corporations have acquired far too much power in the United States.
articles.body:
Corporations have acquired far too much power in the United States. The Supreme Court has given them the same rights as individuals, but without citizens’ responsibilities. The court also allows companies to buy influence by pumping unlimited anonymous cash into political campaigns. Meanwhile, our transactional president seems to peddle favors to corporate donors as if government were a garage sale.

First, elect a Congress willing to investigate and punish grift, graft, pay-to-play government, bribery and extortion.

Second, boycott the companies that have capitulated to President Trump, enriched him and helped him destroy important institutions.

First, expand the No Kings campaign. The mass demonstrations against Trump’s monarchical proclivities could turn their attention to the kingmakers: the companies that enable him with money and capitulation.

Corporations are not immune to market forces, as Disney and ABC found last year when they pulled comedian Jimmy Kimmel off the air. A 2019 study published in the Southern Economic Journal examined 125 U.S. consumer boycotts between 1978 and 2017. It found statistically significant negative effects on the stock market performance of targeted companies.

Second, we must widen the fossil fuel divestment movement. Since 2011, the divest-reinvest movement has urged investors to sell fossil fuel shares and invest in clean energy. So far, more than 1,700 institutions representing nearly $41 trillion in total managed assets have signed up.

One objective is to revoke the “social license of the fossil fuel industry” by highlighting how the fuels harm society. Research suggests some success in shifting public perceptions about the fuels. Fossil fuels still supply more than 80 percent of the world’s primary energy, but clean energy is attracting about twice as much global investment as coal, oil and gas. A similar movement could taint the brands of corporations that help Trump enrich himself, sabotage important institutions, and undermine democracy. On the flip side, the movement could praise companies that pledge to avoid Trump’s swamp.

Third, build a public database of Trump’s corporate collaborators. Several organizations track corporate and personal contributions to Trump, his projects and his organizations, and how they appear connected to the administration’s actions. Watchdogs could collaborate on a central website that lists the corporations and business leaders who have collaborated with, contributed to or capitulated to Trump, along with the administration’s actions on their behalf.

The website should avoid defamatory allegations against Trump or his donors, but it should list cases based on laws that prohibit federal employees from betraying the public trust or even appearing to have conflicts of interest. The Constitution’s emoluments clause applies to the president, and bribery is specifically listed as an impeachable offense. Other laws prohibit private entities from bribing or giving anything of value to a public official in exchange for government actions.

Who are these companies? Public Citizen lists corporations that gave millions of dollars for Trump’s lavish 2025 inauguration. They included Amazon, Apple, AT&T, Bank of America, Chevron, Citigroup, Coinbase, Google, Ford, GM and Goldman Sachs. Contributions totaled more than $245 million . The Brennan Center for Justice found “substantial donations coinciding with advantageous policy or personnel decisions by the Trump administration, as well as an unprecedented number of refunds and millions of dollars in donations for which the true sources are not entirely clear.”

Public Citizen also reports that the Trump administration canceled enforcement actions for alleged lawbreaking by 205 corporations . Ninety companies have or had ties to Trump or his administration.

The Washington Post says that Trump’s White House ballroom project received 67 donations above $10,000 as of September, totaling $333 million. Companies or their affiliates that gave more than $3 million included Meta, Apple, Nvidia, Blackrock, Coinbase, NextEra Energy, Lockheed Martin, Amazon, Cisco, Microsoft, Caterpillar, T-Mobile and Comcast. “The vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government,” the Post said.

The group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington reports that 15 companies have given money to three or more of Trump’s pet projects, with Meta, Amazon, Coinbase and Google-YouTube contributing most often. The group says that all 15 had business before the government or sought something from Trump.

Trump-related lawsuits so far reportedly have leveraged more than $90 million from corporations that capitulated and settled out of court. Meta reportedly paid $25 million, YouTube-Alphabet $24.5 million, Paramount-CBS $16 million, Twitter-X $10 million, and ABC News-Disney $15 million.

Congress will look into some of this if Democrats prevail in next month’s election. But that shouldn’t stop the American people from using their purses against the companies contributing to the most corrupt president in the nation’s history.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: El-Sayed to Trump: ‘I will be Senator Mohamed to you bro’
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Sunday fired back at President Trump’s anti-Muslim rhetoric toward him, telling supporters that the president will be referring to him as “Senator Mohamed” if he wins in November. “I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name,” El-Sayed said at a…
articles.body:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Sunday fired back at President Trump’s anti-Muslim rhetoric toward him, telling supporters that the president will be referring to him as “Senator Mohamed” if he wins in November.

“I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name,” El-Sayed said at a rally in Grand Rapids, Mich. “He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity. Doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet. He just seems to have trouble pronouncing it when it’s my name.”

“But y’all, I don’t care how he pronounces my name,” he continued. “I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name. Because he can just go on and call me ‘senator’ after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro.”

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate.

Trump has frequently attacked El-Sayed’s faith on the campaign trail, mocking his name and alleging the candidate has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt that has influenced and supported fundamentalist movements across the region.

The president has accused the Detroit-area physician of being a “terrorist sympathizer” and a “jihadist,” calling the Michigan Democrat “Mohamed El-Sayed.”

While rallying in Michigan on Sunday for El-Sayed’s opponent, Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), Trump claimed that El-Sayed would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

Trump then likened El-Sayed to the hijackers behind the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks after introducing speaker David Beamer at the rally. Beamer’s son, Todd Beamer, was among the passengers who died on United Flight 93, Reuters reported .

“Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight just like Todd did to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol,” Trump said.

El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, is Muslim and was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents.

Rogers has also made claims tying El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, saying at Sunday’s rally that the group “celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year. Abdul El-Sayed’s.”

“Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker pressed Rogers on NBC News about Trump’s past remarks calling El-Sayed a “violent terrorist” and whether he agreed with the president.

“No, I don’t,” Rogers said. “I’ve never called him a terrorist. I’ve never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul. I mean, he’s a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don’t like America. I think those are issues people ought to decide their election on.”

Rogers said El-Sayed “just won’t answer the question” about any alleged connection with the Muslim Brotherhood and told Welker that his opponent “is getting money from groups that support the Muslim Brotherhood. Money from groups that support Hamas and Hezbollah.”

El-Sayed has vigorously denied any personal ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, though Republicans have dug up past statements by El-Sayed they say are sympathetic to the Islamist movement that briefly took over Egypt in 2012 and 2013.

articles.title: Who has the most at stake in Michigan’s Senate race? It may surprise you.
articles.summary: The stakes may be nearly as high for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and the broader progressive movement she increasingly represents.
articles.body:
Conventional wisdom holds that President Trump has the most at stake in next week’s midterms. Should they win, Democrats have promised investigations, possible impeachment proceedings and sustained oversight that could dominate his final two years in office.

There is truth to that. But the stakes may be nearly as high for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and the broader progressive movement she increasingly represents. Nowhere is that clearer than Michigan, where Ocasio-Cortez has rallied the progressive “Squad” behind Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed.

Ocasio-Cortez transferred $1 million from her campaign account to support El-Sayed, lent him her national platform and campaigned with him not only in Detroit but in Michigan’s Republican-heavy Upper Peninsula — the kind of territory her political theory requires progressives to compete in.

Put simply, Ocasio-Cortez now shares ownership of the result.

Ocasio-Cortez appears to be positioning herself for 2028; her interest in either a Senate campaign or the White House is hardly secret. She has alluded to higher ambitions, built one of Congress’s largest campaign war chests and remained a leading contender on prediction markets .

Viewed through that lens, her calculation is straightforward: Michigan offers perhaps the clearest test of whether a progressive can win a statewide general election in a genuine battleground state that twice voted for Donald Trump. An El-Sayed victory would support her argument, in her own words , that any progressive “can win anywhere.”

There’s also a personal benefit, if she’s right. If El-Sayed wins, even with a strong national environment boosting Democrats, Ocasio-Cortez will receive a considerable boost just as attention turns toward the 2028 primaries.

Conversely, a Mike Rogers victory would deal a serious blow to the argument that candidates from the party’s left can win beyond safely Democratic constituencies. If El-Sayed loses while Democrats lead the generic congressional ballot by slightly more than 8 points and a Republican president has historically weak approval ratings , the setback to Ocasio-Cortez’s case for 2028 will be difficult to dismiss.

The progressive movement , which hailed El-Sayed’s primary victory as proof of concept, would also face legitimate questions, while Democratic moderates would gain evidence that their approach remains more viable nationally.

The counterargument would be obvious: Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), the centrist El-Sayed defeated by only 1 point, was running even with Rogers at a time when El-Sayed trailed him. A loss would make “Stevens would have won” a Democratic refrain for years.

That being said, Ocasio-Cortez may therefore have committed substantial political capital too early and read too much into progressives’ string of summer primary victories.

El-Sayed is a complicated candidate. Republicans have highlighted his association with controversial figures and alleged links to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims he denies. Polling suggests voters remain divided both on him and on the progressive project he represents. A Brookings Institution study of the 2026 primaries found that progressives won only 18 percent of genuinely competitive Democratic contests.

To that end, in Michigan, El-Sayed is running behind other Democrats at both the state and national levels. El-Sayed’s average lead over Rogers is about 2 points, effectively a statistical tie. By comparison, moderate Democrats Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) in Georgia lead their Republican opponents by roughly 10 and 9 points, respectively. Within Michigan, Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson leads Rep. John James (R-Mich.) by nearly 6 points on average.

Whether because of personal concerns, ideology or the attacks on his candidacy, El-Sayed is underperforming moderate Democrats and the top of his own state ticket in a state where Democrats have not lost a Senate race in three decades. As Bloomberg News has suggested , the gap between El-Sayed’s standing and that of Benson and other moderates “could reflect a hesitation among Michigan voters to back a left-wing candidate.”

That is the same question Ocasio-Cortez could face nationally in 2028: Can intense enthusiasm among young, white and college-educated progressives translate into support from the independents and working-class voters who decide battleground states?

Trump and Republicans are leaning heavily into that vulnerability, portraying El-Sayed’s brand of “unapologetic progressivism” as another sign that Democrats have moved too far left. Their attacks have helped turn the race into a referendum on the movement’s broader viability.

That brings the discussion back to the stakes for Ocasio-Cortez and the progressive left. As we have previously argued , Michigan’s importance extends well beyond 2026. If Democrats capture the Senate with El-Sayed providing a decisive victory, the party’s 2028 conversation will tilt toward progressives — and perhaps toward Ocasio-Cortez herself.

An El-Sayed victory would give her perhaps the most important credential she still lacks: evidence that her politics can travel beyond deeply blue areas. If he loses, however, Ocasio-Cortez and her allies will spend the next two years answering charges that their movement cost Democrats a winnable seat — and potentially the Senate majority.

Either way, for Ocasio-Cortez and the progressive movement, the 2028 primary is already underway in Michigan.

Douglas E. Schoen and Carly Cooperman are pollsters and partners with the public opinion company Schoen Cooperman Research based in New York. They are co-authors of the book “ America: Unite or Die . ”

articles.body:
Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R), who is running for Michigan’s open Senate seat, said Sunday he never called opponent Abdul El-Sayed (D) a “terrorist.”

Rogers addressed President Trump’s anti-Muslim rhetoric toward El-Sayed during an interview on “Meet the Press” on NBC News. Host Kristen Welker asked whether Rogers agreed with Trump in calling El-Sayed a “violent terrorist.”

“No, I don’t,” Rogers said. “I’ve never called him a terrorist. I’ve never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul. I mean, he’s a Democratic Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don’t like America. I think those are issues people ought to decide their election on.”

Rogers claimed El-Sayed has dismissed questions about alleged ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt that has influenced and supported fundamentalist movements across the region, and accused Welker of not pressing El-Sayed on the alleged connection.

Welker pointed to El-Sayed writing a letter in 2012 in support of Egyptian protesters against former President Hosni Mubarak and contextualized it with remarks Rogers made around that same time.

“‘Do I think there are moderate Muslim Brotherhood individuals we are going to have to reach out to and talk to? Yes. But we are going to have to watch it carefully,'” she read, quoting Rogers at the time. “Do you acknowledge that at the time, in 2012, you were willing to work with some moderate members, as you said, of the Muslim Brotherhood?”

Rogers said his words were taken “so much out of context” and accused Welker of “letting him [El-Sayed] lie to you.”

“So what happened was, we had relationships where Israel and Egypt had relationships in their intelligence services that the Muslim Brotherhood was trying to undo,” Rogers said after a back-and-forth with Welker. “And what that would’ve meant is more violence in the region. So as chairman of the Intelligence Committee, I said, ‘We’re going to have to find a way to try to not sever that relationship,’ which they did, by the way.”

Rogers later claimed the Muslim Brotherhood supported Abdul’s primary win.

The Michigan Democrat was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents and, if elected, would become the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate. He has vehemently denied any personal ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, though Republicans have dug up past statements by El-Sayed they say are sympathetic to the Islamist movement that briefly took over Egypt in 2012 and 2013.

El-Sayed has hit back at anti-Muslim insults from Trump, who has called El-Sayed “Mohammed” and on Sunday likened him to the hijackers aboard United Flight 93 during the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks.

“I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name,” El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, told supporters in Grand Rapids, Mich., late Sunday.

“But y’all, I don’t care how he pronounces my name,” he added. “I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name. Because he can just go on and call me ‘senator’ after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro.”

articles.title: Corruption might not be the winning issue Democrats expect
articles.summary: Democrats should remember that throughout American history, it has seldom been easy to turn the perceived corruption of one party into an electoral advantage for the other. That is because voters tend to see both parties — and politics itself — as corrupt.
articles.body:
The results of a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released on Oct. 18 show that 66 percent of the American people believe President Trump “is using the presidency to enrich himself.” This follows on the heels of a Fox News survey showing that 88 percent are extremely or very concerned about government corruption, topping a list of issues including inflation, gas prices and health care.

Americans say they trust Democrats more than Republicans to handle each of those issues by “double digits.” And the Post poll contained more bad news for Trump and his party: there has been a steep increase in the percentage of self-identified Republicans and Republican-leaning independents who think the president is using his office to enrich himself.

At first glance, these results would seem to be teeing up a Democratic sweep in the upcoming midterm elections, suggesting the wisdom of the strategy pursued by Democrats across the country in making corruption in Washington a central part of their campaigns.

None has done this better than Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.). In appearance after appearance, he has hammered home the following message: “This is the most corrupt administration of all time, and everybody knows it. While Americans pay more and get less, while our insurance premiums skyrocket and hospitals close down services, while American service members are wounded and killed in action, the first family (is) raking in billions of dollars.”

But Democrats should remember that throughout American history, it has seldom been easy to turn the perceived corruption of one party into an electoral advantage for the other. That is because voters tend to see both parties — and politics itself — as corrupt.

If Democrats want to capitalize on the corruption issue, they need to do more than point the finger of blame at Trump. They need to offer a set of proposals to combat corruption , regardless of who is in office.

So far, they have done a lot of finger-pointing while offering few, if any, proposals.

Part of the problem that Democrats face is that Trump has driven home the message that the Biden administration, including the former president and his son, Hunter, was the most corrupt in American history. As The Washington Post notes , as far back as 2019, Trump was frequently making accusations that when Biden was vice president, he had intervened to stop a Ukrainian prosecutor from “investigating Ukraine’s largest private gas company, Burisma, which had added Biden’s son, Hunter, to its board in 2014.”

Trump has used Hunter Biden as a whipping boy for his claims about the Biden family’s corruption, alleging that Hunter received millions in payments from China as a way to curry favor with his father.

The president has been aided by his allies in Congress as well. In 2023, the Oversight Committee of the House of Representatives claimed that “the Bidens and their associates created over 20 shell companies, raked in over $24 million [dollars] from China and other foreign countries, identified nine members of the Biden family who have participated or benefited from the business schemes, and confirmed that Joe Biden interacted with his family’s business associates at least two dozen times.”

Such accusations, repeated over and over, foster public sentiment that, when it comes to corruption, “everybody does it.” That’s why, as far back as 20 years ago, around 60 percent of the American public believed that corruption was widespread throughout government. Since then, that belief has become even more widespread .

Large swathes of the public in this country seemed to have imbibed the teachings of a British aristocrat, Lord John Dahlberg Acton, who in 1887 wrote to Mandell Creighton, an Anglican bishop, “I cannot accept your canon that we are to judge Pope and King, unlike other men, with a favorable presumption that they did no wrong. If there is any presumption, it is the other way against holders of power, increasing as the power increases.”

“Power,” he added, “tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely. Great men are almost always bad men.”

If all great men are bad men, then, it is not surprising that voters generally do not use their votes to punish leaders whom they believe are corrupt. Instead, the more they hear that leaders are corrupt, the more resigned they become to that fact.

In March, the Brennan Center for Justice wrote that “One of the most destructive effects of corruption is that it depresses democratic participation. Study after study demonstrates that people are significantly less likely to vote when they view their political system as corrupt.”

“This reduced political engagement,” the center continues, “is most pronounced among citizens who otherwise exhibit the strongest civic habits: Those who vote most consistently, consume the most political information, and have the highest capacity to mobilize are especially vulnerable to resignation when they believe corruption is pervasive.”

This is not to say that Democrats should stop talking about corruption in the remaining days before the midterm elections. But as they do so, they need to realize that public concern about corruption in itself may not readily translate into votes for Democratic candidates for the House and Senate.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.
