articles.title: McConnell: Latest Trump bid to end Russia-Ukraine war ‘certain to fail’
articles.summary: Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) is warning that President Trump’s efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine by “coddling” Russian President Vladimir Putin and limiting assistance to Kyiv is “certain to fail.” McConnell, who had been largely quiet on the issue of the war after Ukraine lost full access to the satellite-based Starshield network,…
articles.body:
Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) is warning that President Trump’s efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine by “coddling” Russian President Vladimir Putin and limiting assistance to Kyiv is “certain to fail.”

McConnell, who had been largely quiet on the issue of the war after Ukraine lost full access to the satellite-based Starshield network, which provoked an uproar in Washington, is now speaking out forcefully against Trump’s handling of the conflict.

McConnell, the chair of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, blasted Trump for claiming that Russia “has been fine on Ukraine” when the president was asked about Russian violations of an energy ceasefire.

“This is factually wrong, strategically naive and morally bankrupt. His obsequious accommodation of Russia, rewarding the aggressor with sanctions relief, won’t persuade Mr. Putin to stop. History shows that such behavior emboldens Russia’s autocrat, who sees it as weakness,” he wrote in an op-ed published Sunday by The Wall Street Journal.

McConnell warned that by slowing U.S. military assistance and intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Trump risks making the same mistake former President Biden made in June of 2021 when he withheld U.S. military aid for fear of provoking Russia.

“Threatening to withhold security and intelligence assistance or access to crucial satellite communications systems won’t materially weaken Ukraine’s will to defend itself, but it may allow Mr. Putin to make battlefield headway that had until now been out of reach. This could prolong the war, not shorten it,” McConnell wrote.

And the Senate Republican panned Trump’s deal with Putin announced earlier this month to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel into the United States, a move that prompted pushback from GOP lawmakers on Capitol Hill.

“When Russia’s limited supply of diesel has changed hands, it will have done little to bring down prices at the pump,” McConnell observed, alluding to the fact that the average price of diesel is still more than $6 per gallon in the U.S.

McConnell also dismissed Trump special envoy Steve Witkoff’s declaration that Putin is a “humanitarian” after the Russian leader agreed to release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was wrongfully detained and held in captivity for more than four years.

“If the president means what he says about ending the conflict, he should look to the wisdom of the American people, not naive businessmen who seem to think diplomacy entails fawning over adversaries. Mr. Putin is many things, but he is no humanitarian,” he wrote.

The senior senator from Kentucky argued that allowing Putin to make territorial inroads into Ukraine and to expand Russia’s influence over both Ukraine and Europe would hurt U.S. interests over the long term.

“A Russian victory would have far worse consequences for our economic and national security and our global influence than temporarily high diesel prices,” he said.

He also emphasized that Putin has directed cyberattacks against U.S. government agencies and helped Iran target U.S. personnel and facilities in the Middle East.

“He is an ally of Xi Jinping. He will continue to seize opportunities to weaken America—and Europe,” McConnell said, referring to China’s president.

“The Continent is our biggest trading partner and an engine of American economic growth. An outcome to this war that makes it easier for Russia to threaten Europe harms our own interests,” he added.

McConnell said the U.S. also has much to learn from battlefield innovations Ukraine is making in drone warfare and cautioned the Trump administration not to spurn those lessons.

“Ukraine’s innovation on the battlefield against a more powerful aggressor makes its value as a partner obvious,” he said.

“The Pentagon officials involved in restricting U.S. assistance to Ukraine should explain how abandoning the ‘Silicon Valley of warfare’ and the world’s experts in battlefield drone innovation will help America achieve drone dominance,” he added.

McConnell concluded by asserting that most Senate Republicans support Ukraine and oppose appeasing Russia and its allies, China, North Korea and Iran.

He advised Trump to keep this in mind as he prepares to push through a defense spending package in the lame-duck Congress.

“Passing this agenda will require working with Republicans who know the difference between the good guys and the bad guys. Ending the obeisance to Mr. Putin may be table stakes for the end-of-year legislation. The president should plan accordingly,” he warned.

articles.title: What is voter roll-off and could it play a role in who wins the election this year?
articles.summary: When the votes are finally tallied at the end of an election, it’s normal to see the total number of votes cast in the races at the top of the ticket are slightly higher compared to the races at the bottom. It’s known as voter roll-off.
articles.body:
AUSTIN (Nexstar) — When the votes are finally tallied at the end of an election, it’s normal to see the total number of votes cast in the races at the top of the ticket are slightly higher compared to the races at the bottom. It’s known as voter roll-off.

Mark Jones, a fellow in political science at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, said you normally see voter roll-off as a top-down flow on the ballot.

“As people get to the lower races on the ballot, they tend to stop voting,” Jones explained. “It gets really bad often when they get to county level offices or judicial offices at the district or county level, because they don’t know who these candidates are and they stop voting.”

Almost everybody will know the top of the ticket races on their ballot. Those include the race for U.S. Senate between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton; the gubernatorial race between Democrat Gina Hinojosa and Republican Greg Abbott; and to some extent, the race for Lt. Governor between Democrat Vikki Goodwin and Republican Dan Patrick.

But as voters start making their way down the statewide ballot, they will likely not know every candidate running for offices like Land Commissioner, Railroad Commissioner, or even Attorney General. And there are polls to back this up.

The University of Houston Hobby School of Public Affairs released a poll of 2,000 likely voters last week. The poll found that at least 50% of those likely voters did not know enough about 10 statewide candidates to have a negative or positive opinion about them.

Nathan Johnson is a Democratic state senator who is running to be the next Attorney General of Texas. The poll found that 71% of people did not know enough about him, and 50% did not know enough about his opponent, Mayes Middleton, who is also a state senator.

Dawn Buckingham is a former Republican state senator and the current Land Commissioner of Texas who oversees roughly 13 million acres of public land in the Lone Star State. But the poll found 73% of people do not know enough about her, and 78% do not know enough about her opponent, Benjamin Flores.

Jones said the numbers jump to the 80%-90% range when people are asked about judicial offices. It’s regularly so high that Jones said he and his team have stopped asking people about their opinions on judicial candidates.

Some people decide to leave areas of the ballot blank when they do not know the candidates, but others will still cast a vote on important positions when they know very little of the candidates or their policies. Jones said the decision is mostly based off partisan politics.

“If a voter who gets to say the Office of Land Commissioner and has no idea who the candidates are, they tend to revert to their partisanship because one piece of information that is on the ballot, even if they don’t know who these candidates are, is if they are a Republican, a Democrat or a Libertarian,” Jones explained.

In past elections in Texas, voter roll-off did not play a pivotal role in determining the outcome of the race. Voter roll-off usually accounts for a 1%-2% drop-off in votes, and the margin of victories in past midterm elections were much higher. Take a look at the past two midterm cycles:

But Jones believes voter roll-off could be a factor this election cycle because of how competitive the races are up and down the ballot.

“It’s quite possible in some of the down-ballot races — say for Railroad Commissioner in particular, which is I think the second most competitive race after the US Senate — that there you can see roll-off making the difference between victory and defeat for one of the two candidates,” Jones explained.

The UH poll from last week has French with a 2 point advantage over Rosenthal with still 10% of likely voters undecided in that race.

Jones also believes this year we may see a smaller vote count at the top of the ticket in the U.S. Senate race if some Republican voters decide not to cast a vote because of their dislike for Ken Paxton.

articles.title: Ozempic users may face protein, vitamin D deficiencies, experts warn
articles.summary: As GLP-1 drugs help people eat less, doctors are increasingly concerned about what patients may be missing nutritionally.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Patients prescribed Ozempic and other GLP-1 medications may be at risk for nutritional deficiencies, according to recent studies.

Because GLP-1 medications help people lose weight by reducing appetite and slowing digestion, patients often eat less, increasing the risk of nutrient gaps and prompting concern among doctors and nutrition researchers.

Research points to several common areas of concern, including protein, fiber, vitamin B12, vitamin D, electrolytes, and nutrients vital for maintaining healthy muscle mass and connective tissue.

Am I likely to be protein deficient on Ozempic?

An obesity study found that 43% of GLP-1 users consumed inadequate amounts of protein during a trial period.

Experts at the University of Cambridge have expressed concern that people prescribed newer weight-loss medications may not be receiving proper nutritional guidance to support healthy weight loss.

A research review found that GLP-1 users consume 16% to 39% fewer calories than those taking a placebo.

Given their decreased calorie intake, users can have difficulty getting enough protein and micronutrients in their diets.

Doctors recommend consulting a registered dietitian nutritionist to help improve diet quality.

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics maintains a database of nutrition professionals , allowing people to search by insurance, location and specialty.

Research suggests GLP-1 users are most likely to experience vitamin D deficiencies. A large-scale study found that 13.6% of participants were affected.

Another recent study, published in the journal Childhood Obesity, found vitamin D deficiency was the most common deficiency among children taking GLP-1 medications, affecting 12.4% of participants after one year of treatment.

articles.title: Open enrollment begins: What Medicare beneficiaries need to know for 2027
articles.summary: From GLP-1 drug prices to higher deductibles, several Medicare changes could affect seniors’ wallets in 2027.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Open enrollment for Medicare plans is underway, and several changes are going into effect in 2027 that could affect your health care coverage. Medicare beneficiaries can now change their health and drug coverage plans for the upcoming year through Dec. 7.

What changes are going into effect in 2027?

Changes to Medicare next year include new negotiated drug prices, lower prices for weight-loss drugs, and higher deductibles and out-of-pocket caps.

For Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage, the out-of-pocket limit will be $2,400 in 2027, up from $2,100 in 2026.

The standard deductible for Part D prescription drug coverage will be $700, up from $615 in 2026.

Additionally, new negotiated prices for 15 additional drugs will take effect next year. Among them are certain GLP-1 medications, including Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.

Other medications include Ellipta, Xtandi, Pomalyst, Ibrance, Ofev, Trelegy, Linzess, Calquence, Austedo and Austedo XR, Breo Ellipta, Tradjenta, Xifaxan, Vraylar, Janumet and Janumet XR, and Otezla, according to Newsweek.

The Medicare Part B premium is projected to increase to $209.50 per month, up from $202.90 in 2026, according to the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report. The annual Part B deductible is projected to increase from $283 to about $292.

Retirees are set to receive their largest Social Security cost-of-living adjustment in four years, but higher Medicare Part B premiums could offset some of the increase.

The 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, announced this week , will increase the average Social Security retirement benefit by $75 a month beginning in January, or about $900 over the course of the year.

After the 3.6% COLA, the average monthly benefit for retired workers is expected to reach $2,170 in January 2027, according to the Social Security Administration.

But that’s just the average. Workers who qualify for the maximum benefit and claim at full retirement age can receive up to $4,188 per month.

If the Medicare trustees’ projection is correct, the standard Part B premium would increase from $202.90 per month in 2026 to $209.50 in 2027, a 3.25% increase compared with a nearly 10% jump this year.

articles.title: The 3 approaches to daylight saving time considered this year, and what happened to them
articles.summary: There were three possible approaches the U.S. could have taken this year regarding seasonal time change. Instead, our clocks will fall back as usual next month.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – In just a week, our clocks will fall back an hour as daylight saving time comes to an end. With it will come early sunrises and sunsets, and potentially some health benefits .

If some lawmakers had their way, however, the seasonal time change could have looked a lot differently this fall.

The U.S. nearly locked its clocks on permanent daylight saving time after the House passed the Sunshine Protection Act, sending it off to the Senate with support from President Trump. But the Senate adjourned without taking any action and isn’t expected back until after Election Day. (The legislation doesn’t have a “clear path forward,” though, according to Senate Majority Leader John Thune.)

Had the legislation taken effect, daylight saving time could have become permanent this year, and most U.S. clocks — Hawaii and most of Arizona are already on permanent standard time — would not be falling back in November. Several of our Canadian neighbors enacted permanent daylight saving time this year and will not set their clocks back next weekend.

The U.S. could have taken a different approach that would have set the clocks back an hour in November, as usual, but left them there permanently.

In July, the bipartisan “Sunshine for Our Kids Act” was introduced in the House. The bill calls for year-round standard time in the U.S. , though it would allow states the option to make daylight saving time permanent, an option not currently available to them without action by Congress.

If standard time were to become permanent, our clocks would not “spring forward” an hour in March. Our winters would feel as they do now, but the sun would rise and set an hour earlier than it currently does in spring, summer, and early fall.

The Sunshine for Our Kids Act was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce in July and remains there as of late October.

A third, less common approach to seasonal time change was also suggested this year: “half-daylight saving time.”

Under the Daylight Act of 2026, introduced in the House in February, our clocks would, essentially, fall back 30 minutes in November rather than a full 60 minutes. (If it took effect before March, clocks would spring forward 30 minutes instead of a full 60.) The twice-a-year changing of the clocks would also cease.

While it would be much less drastic than changing by an hour, you would likely notice a difference . Not only would sunrises and sunsets shift , but any international interactions — business, flights, or even crossing the Canadian border while visiting Niagara Falls — would have to account for unusual time zones .

That bill was similarly referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, where it remains as of October.

Also introduced in Congress were two bills that would give states the option to observe year-round daylight saving time, action nearly 20 states have been awaiting . Neither bill progressed out of committee.

For now, our clocks will fall back on the earliest possible date , Nov. 1.

articles.title: Trump and Vance accelerate downward political spiral
articles.summary: Senior political analyst Juan Williams criticizes several candidates in the 2026 midterm elections for employing increasingly unethical and deceptive political advertising tactics.
articles.body:
“Politics ain’t beanbag,” is a famous warning to politicians. They have to tough as the toughest baseball players to win, throwing hardballs at opponents and sliding with their spikes up. Well, the 2026 midterms have now gone from hardball to lowball.

Here is a list of scummy political advertising, complete with despicable lies.

Let’s save the most reprehensible for last.

First, right-wing smear merchants, aided by Elon Musk’s X platform , trashed Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) with wretchedly false claims. They said the Democrat left the campaign trail for treatment at an Ohio hospital for the insane.

It was a despicable lie. Talarico stopped campaigning while recovering from the flu.

The lie was a diversion from the multiple scandals tarring Talarico’s opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

The truth about Paxton is that a Republican-controlled Texas House impeached him in 2023 . His wife filed for divorce on “Biblical grounds.” He has offered no credible explanation for how, as a state government employee, he amassed a multimillion-dollar real estate portfolio reportedly encompassing 15 properties .

His own senior staff reported his conduct to the FBI. Even some leading Texas Republicans are repulsed. Members of the Bush family — Barbara Bush and Neil Bush — are supporting Talarico. Second in the race to the bottom is the Muslim hating attacks on Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), his Republican opponent, portrays El-Sayed as a terrorist sympathizer and supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood. Rogers is making an ugly appeal to Islamophobia, trading on the bigoted idea that American Muslims have terrorist sympathies.

Rogers is willing to exploit that ugly, hateful sentiment by connecting El Sayed’s mother and relatives to social media posts that have nothing to do with El Sayed. Ads made using artificial intelligence show a fabricated El Sayed laughing at calls for “Death to America.”

Odious lies about Muslims, so poisonously divisive, still resonate 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.

But that is not the winner for the lowest act in this lineup of slander of 2026. That dishonor goes to Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy (R). His campaign ran an advertisement in which the elderly mother of his gubernatorial opponent, Amy Acton (D), accuses the Democrat of lying about her childhood traumas.

Ramaswamy’s political attack has no mention of Acton’s stepfather being charged with abusing a 12-year-old girl. Acton has identified herself as that child. Acton’s mother sided with the man charged with abusing her daughter. Ramaswamy ignored public records showing that Acton’s stepfather was indicted.

The mother lost custody of Acton and her brother while remaining married to the accused abuser, who left the state and failed to appear in court.

Acton’s younger brother, Philip Stearns, lashed the Ramaswamy ad as a “despicable low.” Stearns described Ramaswamy as “a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”

Stearns said it was unbelievable that Ramaswamy would “turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point.”

Leading Republican women also castigated Ramaswamy.

“This ad is going to go down as the most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season,” Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) told CNN . She added that Ramaswamy has “managed to limbo under the lowest bar of decency in this country.”

Instead of retracting and apologizing for the ad, Ramaswamy’s campaign announced a $4 million push behind the ad. President Trump advised him to “keep it up” by giving it more TV time. Vice President JD Vance dismissed objections from fellow Republicans as “whining.”

Vance added to the contemptible attack on Action by saying at a rally earlier this month that she is a “crazy person,” and possibly a drunk. Here is Vance: “I did promise Amy that I would meet her at a bar later. I understand she is into that kind of thing.”

Child abuse has been a dark recurring issue in these midterms. The Ramaswamy episode comes as Republicans in Ohio are spending millions to reelect Rep. Max Miller (R). His former wife has accused him of abusing her and their young daughter. The child’s grandfather, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio), has called Miller unfit to serve and demanded his resignation. Yet the Republican-aligned Congressional Leadership Fund has booked more than $5 million in television advertising in the race .

In a 1993 essay, Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan (D-N.Y.) famously coined the phrase “defining deviancy downward.” President Trump with his infamous claim to grab women by the genitals and involvement with a porn actress has accelerated that downward spiral, lowering the bar for wretched political discourse to new nadirs.

Ramaswamy once sent me an angry email after I criticized him in this column for playing racial politics. The column focused on his statement: “I’m sure the boogeyman white supremacists exist somewhere in America. I have just never met him. Never seen one.”

I said he was recklessly pretending there was no more white racism in order to win over white voters. Now Ramaswamy’s offensive attack on Acton makes his earlier lowbrow racist tactics look like nothing. We have sunk far below them.

This is the age of get-in-the-gutter politics.

Juan Williams is senior political analyst for Fox News Channel and a prize-winning civil rights historian. He is the author of the new book “ New Prize for These Eyes: The Rise of America’s Second Civil Rights Movement . “

articles.title: Trump praises ‘proud, resilient’ Libyan people after labeling country ‘terror-infested’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday praised Libya’s “proud, resilient” people after calling the African country “terror-infested” at a rally in Georgia. “The Libyan people are proud, resilient, hospitable, and deserving of peace and prosperity,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The United States and Libya share a strong and enduring partnership in combating terrorism, building on our…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday praised Libya’s “proud, resilient” people after calling the African country “terror-infested” at a rally in Georgia.

“The Libyan people are proud, resilient, hospitable, and deserving of peace and prosperity,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “The United States and Libya share a strong and enduring partnership in combating terrorism, building on our historic success in defeating ISIS in Libya together.”

“We respect the Libyan people and the sacrifices that brave Libyans made fighting ISIS, the common enemy of both our peoples, but Libya cannot remain a corridor for illegal migration, and this must end now,” Trump continued.

The president added that the U.S. is committed to strengthening its relationship with Libya and stands “with the Libyan people as they transition toward successful national elections.”

The post stands in stark contrast to Trump’s comments at a rally in Perry, Ga., stumping for state Republicans, including Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) in his race to unseat Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.).

“Jon Ossoff personally sponsored a bill to bring armies of migrants from terror-infested countries like Libya, Yemen, Haiti, Somalia. Remember what I called them? ‘S—hole countries,'” Trump said, according to Reuters , referring to highly criticized remarks he made during his first term in 2018.

The Libyan Foreign Ministry blasted Trump’s comments at the rally and said they “undermine the dignity of its people or diminish their standing.” The Foreign Ministry also summoned a senior U.S. diplomat to protest Trump’s remarks at the campaign event, Business Insider Africa reported Monday.

The Trump administration has sought to restore a U.S. presence in Libya since the fall of dictator Moammar Gadhafi in 2011 and the subsequent civil war.

The State Department in July informed Congress that it planned to reopen the U.S. Embassy in Libya. There is no active U.S. Embassy in the country, and the State Department has urged Americans not to travel to Libya .

Trump’s original “s—hole countries” comments, said during a meeting about protections for immigrants from several countries, caused a massive stir. The president asked why the U.S. was “having all these people from s—hole countries come here,” according to multiple reports at the time.

The president doubled down on the statement and did not apologize, The Associated Press reported. Lawmakers and world leaders blasted the remark as racist and offensive, with Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) confirming he heard Trump make the remark at the meeting. Two Republican lawmakers said they did not recall hearing Trump use the term at the meeting.

articles.title: Trump: Maher a ‘coward who is afraid to tell the truth’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday exploded at comedian Bill Maher in a Truth Social post calling him a “coward who is afraid to tell the truth.” Trump launched his post by accusing Maher of being a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” and that his HBO show “Real Time” was “not ‘HOT’ anymore.” “He isn’t worth it,” Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday exploded at comedian Bill Maher in a Truth Social post calling him a “coward who is afraid to tell the truth.”

Trump launched his post by accusing Maher of being a “COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER” and that his HBO show “Real Time” was “not ‘HOT’ anymore.”

“He isn’t worth it,” Trump wrote later in the post. “Bill: Don’t call anymore. It’s useless. … You’re also a coward who is afraid to tell the truth about how well our Country is running because of your few ‘fans,’ and how badly the Dumocrats have done, almost destroying the U.S.A.”

“If I hadn’t won the Election, it would be DEAD!” Trump continued. “Also, turn your Laugh Machine off, it’s a joke when they laugh uncontrollably, even when you saynothing funny, and I’m going to have the Republicans not cover you anymore, because they try to talk about you as a guy who is transformative.”

“You’re not transformative, you’re a Loser!” he added.

Last week, Maher attended a dinner with Trump, joined by musician Kid Rock and sports commentator Stephen A. Smith, at the White House. Maher previously dined with Trump last year, and former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt appeared on “Real Time” as a guest last week.

Trump said Maher’s show became “far worse” after the second dinner, and that he “went crazy!”

“Karoline Leavitt was GREAT on the show, but she started with a biased, dumb SLEAZEBAG, asking questions,” Trump wrote. “She defended me, and herself, so well, but couldn’t be comfortable going against Lie after Lie.”

He accused Maher of lying about the Department of Justice’s legal battle with California over its voter rolls, requesting that the state set aside 20,000 ballots for noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections.

“Just in the last few days alone, they found 20,000, and the number could easily go to over 1,000,000,” Trump wrote. “There were so many other falsehoods Bill spewed, but I won’t waste time in FACT CHECKING him. He isn’t worth it.”

The liberal comic has been a longtime critic of Trump’s, though he faced backlash over his dinner with Trump in early 2025 after warning about the results of a second Trump presidency. He defended both dinners with the president, telling viewers on Friday that it allowed him to press Trump on different issues.

“Yeah, I did it again, b‑‑‑‑,” Maher said. “I go and say face-to-face to the man the things you write in articles he’ll never read, but OK. You know what? F‑‑‑ you. I like these dinners.”

“Seinfeld” co-creator Larry David, another vocal Trump critic, notably lampooned Maher’s first dinner with Trump in The New York Times with the op-ed “My Dinner with Adolf,” which Maher accused of being “insulting to 6 million dead Jews.” Both comedians are of Jewish descent.

articles.title: The power of faith meets the corruption of power
articles.summary: Trump’s religious right collaborators and enablers have done great damage to Christian witness.
articles.body:
I am an American who believes President Donald Trump and his political collaborators and enablers have done catastrophic damage to our country. And I am a Christian who believes that Trump’s religious right collaborators and enablers have done great damage to Christian witness.

I am hopeful that the upcoming midterm elections will be a turning point away from both MAGA destruction and the religious right’s corruption.

What could make people more cynical about politics than Republicans who loudly declare their devotion to the Constitution but abandon the rule of law, embrace or excuse Trump’s self-dealing and devote themselves to making it harder for people to vote? And what could make people more skeptical about Christianity than religious leaders who pose as champions of truth while embracing or excusing Trump’s lying, cruelty and relentless attacks on the dignity of his political opponents?

How about leaders who preach that political engagement is a Christian duty, but then viciously smear Christians who don’t share their belief that Trump was anointed by God?

The attacks on Christians like U.S. Senate candidates James Talarico and Adam Hamilton — a Presbyterian seminarian and the pastor of the nation’s largest Methodist Church — have been revolting and revealing.

MAGA pastors and pundits have savaged the faith of Talarico, who has respectfully challenged Republican colleagues in the state legislature who fly a banner of Christianity while enacting harmful policies. For that he has been insulted as a “fake” Christian and much worse — a “ tool for the devil ” and “ son of Satan .” All while avowedly Christian leaders rally around Ken Paxton, one of the most notoriously corrupt figures in American politics.

Vice President JD Vance, who notably tried to school the pope on the application of Catholic social teaching, outright lied about Andrew Hamilton’s faith and declared that the author of 30 books about Christianity was not a real Christian. It was as pathetic as it was dishonest.

Religious right leaders have spent decades building political power by claiming ownership of faith, family and freedom — all while pushing agendas that have made people’s lives more fragile and less free. Along the way they’ve attacked progressive leaders whose Christian faith has inspired their justice-seeking activism and public service, from Martin Luther King Jr. to Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.).

When Trump came along, they made a deal with the Donald. During the 2016 election, he knew he had to overcome conservative Christian skepticism about his greed and amorality. So, he proposed a transaction. If they could convince their followers to put him in the White House, he would make them more politically powerful than they had ever been.

That sounded to one evangelical writer like the deal that the devil offered in the Bible story about Satan tempting Jesus in the wilderness with earthly power. Religious leaders shouldn’t take the deal that Jesus rejected , he wrote. But they took the deal, and they’ve been drunk with the power and access that Trump has given them.

Polls suggest that plenty of American Christians, including many who voted for Trump in the past, are done with his bigotry, bullying and indifference to the ways his policies are making life more difficult and less affordable for millions of families.

That gives me hope. But there are good reasons not to be complacent.

Religious right leaders are doubling down on their devotion to Trump. Trump’s faith advisor Paula White and her National Faith Advisory Board are working overtime to energize pastors who are willing to turn their churches into get-out-the-vote operations for Republican candidates.

In addition, polls may not be capturing the impact of the religious right’s big data and big money driven voter turnout operations that are spending tens of millions of dollars to try to preserve Republican majorities in Congress and ensure that Trump can continue to operate without oversight or accountability.

And I’m afraid that whatever illegal schemes Trump’s team might employ to interfere with the elections or refuse to honor the results, he will be able to count on the support of many of the religious right figures who have backed his other lies.

If Trump tries again, with the backing of Republican leaders, to subvert the Constitution and carry out a coup against the expressed will of the American people, it will be a severe challenge to our already strained democratic institutions. And it will be a supreme test of character for Trump’s Christian supporters, who will have to choose between their commitment to democracy and their loyalty to its corrupter-in-chief.

If we find ourselves facing such a crisis and moment of truth, I hope those Trump supporters might consider one of the most famous questions Jesus asked of his followers: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”

Sadly, I am not confident about how they will answer that question. So, the rest of us must be prepared to defend our democracy and continue to fight for the soul of our country.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way .

articles.title: Tina Peters plans Supreme Court bid while convictions are upheld in Colorado
articles.summary: Tina Peters’ attorney, Peter Ticktin, told FOX31 that he is preparing to take her case to the U.S. Supreme Court in hopes of overturning her criminal convictions stemming from a 2021 breach of Mesa County’s election equipment.
articles.body:
DENVER ( KDVR ) — Former Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters is out of prison, but her legal fight is far from over.

Her attorney, Peter Ticktin, told Nexstar’s KDVR that he is preparing to take her case to the Supreme Court in hopes of overturning her criminal convictions stemming from a 2021 breach of Mesa County’s election equipment.

The effort is drawing differing reactions from Peters’ legal team and Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, who says the jury reached the correct verdict.

Peters was convicted in August 2024 on seven criminal counts connected to the election equipment breach. Prosecutors said she helped an unauthorized person gain access to the county’s voting equipment during a software update.

Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted Peters’ prison sentence, but her convictions remain in place.

Attorney said Peters was protecting election records

Ticktin argued that Peters was attempting to preserve election data she believed could be lost during a software update.

He maintains that Peters was fulfilling her responsibilities under federal election record retention laws rather than committing a crime.

“She’s an innocent woman who was doing her duty to America, and she was punished severely for that,” Ticktin told KDVR.

Ticktin argued that federal law should have taken precedence over state restrictions governing access to election equipment.

“If you have to do something to make sure that you abide by a federal statute, even if it violates a state statute, you’re allowed to do that,” Ticktin said.

That interpretation is part of the argument he hopes to bring before the Supreme Court. It has not been accepted as a legal defense to Peters’ convictions.

Ticktin also contended that Peters did not receive a fair trial and that she was prevented from fully presenting her defense to jurors.

After the Colorado Supreme Court declined to review her appeal, Ticktin said his team is preparing to seek review from the nation’s highest court.

“We have until December to file our briefs and we’re working on them now,” Ticktin told KDVR in a follow-up statement.

He said his goal is to overturn the convictions and clear Peters’ criminal record.

Colorado County Clerks Association director defends conviction

Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, disagreed with Ticktin’s argument that Peters needed to take extraordinary measures to preserve election records.

Crane told KDVR that Mesa County election employees had already backed up the records required under state and federal law.

“What the jury got right is that she broke the law. She didn’t need to do what she did,” Crane said.

According to Crane, Peters’ actions went beyond what was necessary to fulfill her responsibilities as county clerk.

He said election officials have established procedures for preserving records and protecting voting equipment.

“Election integrity does not require you to break the law,” Crane said.

Crane also questioned whether the Supreme Court would overturn the verdict.

“It’s tough for me to envision a world in which the Supreme Court would overturn her conviction,” Crane said.

Disagreement over the governor’s decision to commute sentence

Although Peters is no longer serving her original prison sentence, her convictions remain in place.

The Colorado Court of Appeals previously found that Peters’ sentence had been improperly influenced, in part, by her protected speech and ordered further sentencing proceedings.

Crane told FOX31 he believes the governor should have allowed that process to continue before intervening.

“I think Governor Polis got in the way of justice working,” Crane said.

Ticktin, meanwhile, argued that Peters should never have been convicted and that her release does not resolve what he considers an unjust prosecution.

Ticktin said his legal team is working toward a December filing deadline as it prepares to ask the Supreme Court to review Peters’ case.

The court is not required to accept the appeal.

If the justices decline to hear it, Peters’ convictions would remain in place. If they agree to review the case, they could ultimately uphold the convictions, reverse them or send the case back for additional proceedings, depending on the legal questions presented.

A decision to hear the case would not automatically mean Peters’ convictions would be overturned.

Despite those uncertainties, Ticktin expressed confidence in his legal strategy.

“I’m always in it to win it,” Ticktin said. “I don’t see any reason to look at it any other way.”

What could the case mean for Colorado elections?

With the midterm elections approaching, the legal battle is also renewing discussion about election security, accountability and public trust in voting systems.

Ticktin maintains that Peters was trying to protect election records and argues that her prosecution raises questions about how election officials can fulfill their responsibilities when they believe records are at risk.

Crane sees the potential consequences differently.

As executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, Crane said he worries about the message that overturning Peters’ convictions could send to election workers who follow established security procedures.

“It puts a bigger bullseye on the back of election officials who, since 2020, have been standing up and pushing back on these lies,” Crane said.

Crane also emphasized that voters can learn more about election procedures directly from their local election offices.

“You can call your county clerk, sign up for a tour, go do that,” Crane said.

He encouraged voters not to let the legal dispute discourage them from participating in the upcoming election.

“Just make sure you get out and vote,” Crane said.

For now, Peters’ convictions remain in place as her legal team prepares its next filing. Whether the U.S. Supreme Court will agree to review her case remains to be seen.

articles.body:
President Trump said progressive firebrand Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) doesn’t “bug” him much at a Sunday rally in Michigan.

While criticizing Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Mich.), a common foe for the president, Trump struck a more positive tone on Ocasio-Cortez, a popular Democrat and potential 2028 presidential candidate . Ocasio-Cortez is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America and ally to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who has been traveling across the country campaigning for Democrats and criticizing Trump and his administration.

“Somehow I don’t mind AOC that much,” Trump said, using Ocasio-Cortez’s nickname. “I don’t know why, she doesn’t bug me too much.”

Ocasio-Cortez is seen as a potential presidential candidate by Democrats looking to capitalize on the momentum and popularity of progressives like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D). She has said she will weigh whether or not to run for president after the midterm elections but made headlines when she indicated that 2028 might be her one plausible window for a presidential run.

“There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” Ocasio-Cortez told The New York Times . “And you don’t — and just in life in general — life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

The New York lawmaker has consistently polled strongly among the top Democrats weighing a run for the White House, and her decision could change the makeup of the 2028 race. A New York Times/Siena poll taken in mid-October found 6 percent of respondents would vote for Ocasio-Cortez in a primary, placing her behind former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The presidency is not Ocasio-Cortez’s only option. She could decide to pass on a presidential run and challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for his Senate seat instead — or run for reelection in the House.

articles.title: Drone warfare could save NATO
articles.summary: Imagine how Russia would fare against 32 Ukraines.
articles.body:
Since its creation in 1949 , NATO has been history’s most successful and longest lasting military alliance. Now, that is changing — and for the wrong reasons. For the only time in its 77 years, NATO is threatened not only by an external adversary but, frighteningly, from within. And this new threat is very real.

President Donald Trump’s administration has made several unambiguously clear demands on NATO. First, European members must assume greater, if not virtually all, responsibility for the defense of Europe. This will allow the U.S. to focus on its main priorities of homeland defense and averting a Chinese invasion or assault on Taiwan. The Pentagon is also finalizing plans for redeployment of U.S. troops from Europe to reinforce the other two actions.

It is possible that for the first time the next Supreme Allied Commander Europe will be a European, not an American . If that occurs, the link with NATO’s Article Five guarantee that “an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members,” and the U.S. nuclear deterrent, could be severed.

Concurrently, European NATO members are increasingly wary and indeed worried that Russia may launch a military offensive against the alliance. This fear may be voiced to delay possible U.S. troop withdrawals. Some argue Russia could attack the Baltic States and seize an island in the Baltic or Norway’s Svalbard as a fait accompli to break alliance cohesion. Then, Russia would use its sole military advantage of overwhelming nuclear weapons superiority to prevent any NATO response.

Meanwhile, Russian “ active measures ” to disrupt and divide the alliance continue with cyber strikes, propaganda, sabotage, drone and aircraft territorial violations and threats to use nuclear weapons.

Given this dual challenge to the alliance’s future, what can and should NATO do to maintain its relevance? In addition to taking immediate counters to Russian active measures, only one viable option exists to prevent a possible fatal rift in the alliance: a program to integrate unmanned air, land and sea drones to NATO’s defense kits. Unmanned is a bit misleading. People will still need to sustain, repair, maintain and deploy unmanned systems.

Iran and Ukraine have shown how war can be transformed by cheap drones in large numbers. That a relatively tiny state could fight a far more powerful Russian enemy to a standstill for nearly five years is a tribute to Ukrainian courage, resolve and employment of drone-based war. As quickly as possible, NATO must follow suit but with a new strategy that capitalizes on the operational and cost-effective asymmetries offered by unmanned resources.

NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander, U.S, Air Force Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, laid out his theory of victory in Poland last week. In a speech that has not been released, the general called for a strategy to “ blunt, block and break” any Russian attack. This concept is a variant of a “ Porcupine Strategy ” that we have previously proposed.

A Porcupine Strategy would make any initial aggression so costly it would become unacceptable. Here, vast numbers of inexpensive unmanned vehicles are central. NATO’s 32 members can deploy many tens of thousands of unmanned vehicles on its flanks and in central Europe.

Imagine how Russia would fare against 32 Ukraines.

Unmanned vehicles would be stationed throughout Europe. In the northern flank, the United Kingdom, Greenland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and Finland would base these units. Likewise, in the Baltic, Mediterranean and Black Seas, the Balts, Greece, the Balkans, Turkey, Bulgaria and Romania could serve as unmanned bases. In central Europe, unmanned vehicles will be powerful blunters, blockers and breakers against any aggression.

The strategic value of unmanned vehicles extends far beyond a Porcupine Defense. They will reduce the demand for U.S. manned forces in Europe and absorb any redeployments or shifts to Asia. Unmanned vehicles operating across the entire European continent, in and over the land and under the oceans, would make a Porcupine Defense a highly cost-effective means for preventing and disrupting any attack Moscow might contemplate.

Virtually every military is scrambling to determine where and how unmanned vehicles can augment or replace traditional defenses. Lessons from the war in Ukraine are largely unique to that conflict. However, the application of unmanned resources, in conjunction with artificial intelligence, offers NATO the most economically sound strategy to deal with both the old and newer threats.

The question is whether NATO will exploit this opportunity.

Harlan Ullman Ph.D. is chairman of a private company, and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. Field Marshal the Lord David Richards was the United Kingdom’s former chief of the General Staff and chief of Defense. Their next book due out this winter, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos.”

articles.title: White House Halloween party to feature Trump Accounts coloring books, Be Best cards
articles.summary: There will be more than pumpkins and candy at the White House’s Halloween celebration — this year’s fright-filled festivities are also poised to scare up some support for Trump Accounts. The first lady’s press office on Monday announced plans for the annual spooky tradition at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. President Trump and Melania Trump will hand…
articles.body:
There will be more than pumpkins and candy at the White House’s Halloween celebration — this year’s fright-filled festivities are also poised to scare up some support for Trump Accounts.

The first lady’s press office on Monday announced plans for the annual spooky tradition at 1600 Pennsylvania Ave.

President Trump and Melania Trump will hand out commemorative candies as they welcome “trick or treaters of all ages” to the South Lawn on Thursday afternoon for the pre-Halloween shindig. The event, which typically draws thousands of costumed visitors, is open to ticketholders, which include military and law enforcement families, the children of administration officials and foster and adoptive families, according to the White House.

The South Portico of the White House will feature trick-or-treat booths and spooky decorations, along with Halloween tunes performed by the U.S. Air Force Strolling Strings.

In addition to sweet treats, children will also be receiving coloring books from the Treasury Department “as part of its promotion of Trump Accounts for young trick or treaters.”

The Trump administration launched the president’s eponymous newborn investment program, which open federal savings accounts for qualifying children born between 2025 and 2028, earlier this year.

Melania Trump’s Be Best initiative — which the first lady kicked off in 2018 — will also be represented. The U.S. Postal Service “will provide toy mail trucks and facilitate a Be Best post card station for children.”

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is also expected to go big with gourds at the jack-o-lantern-friendly fête. The USDA “will have a giant pumpkin photo opportunity and hand out mini pumpkins from American farmers.”
